settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The identity `!=` test with a subsequent `.equals` is a common pattern meant to handle interned strings, and in the common http(s) case where both hosts are interned the behavior is correct.
A `se` is produced whenever docHost == null AND the identity test is true (docHost != scriptHost, i.e. a null vs non-null host) - lines 87-88 do handle the null-vs-non-null case.
The data-protocol exemption (lines 89-93) may be an intentional, documented relaxation for inline scripts.
No caller in the read spans was analyzed to confirm that an attacker can actually reach the constructor with a null-host docURL.
candidates.description: DefaultScriptSecurity's constructor compares the document host and the script host using reference identity (docHost != scriptHost) OR'ed with a null-aware equals test. The security decision is made only inside the `if ((docHost != scriptHost) && ((docHost == null) || (!docHost.equals(scriptHost))))` block (lines 87-88). When the two host strings are the same interned/identical reference, or when docHost is non-null and docHost.equals(scriptHost) is true, the block is not entered and `se` stays null, so checkLoadScript() returns silently. More importantly for null hosts: if docHost is null, the second clause `(docHost == null)` evaluates true, but that only broadens when the block is entered; the guard is bypassed entirely only when the identity test is false. Because `ParsedURL.getHost()` can return null for several URL shapes (e.g. file:, data:, and relative/opaque references), and because scripts embedded with the data protocol are explicitly exempted (lines 89-93), a document that is itself loaded from a null-host URL can accept a script reference to a different location without triggering the cross-host SecurityException. The intent of the class (only allow scripts from the same server as the document) is therefore not enforced for null-host inputs. This is reported as a candidate; traceability to a concrete attacker-controlled entry point is not established in the read source.
missing_evidence: The full constructor control flow for the case docHost == null AND scriptHost == null (does the block get entered?).
Whether an attacker controlling the SVG document can force a null docURL host in deployment paths (transcoder vs swing vs browser).
The exact behavior of ParsedURL.getHost() for the relevant URL forms, which is outside the read spans.
How UserAgentAdapter/BridgeContext select DefaultScriptSecurity and whether embedding/no-load variants take precedence.
preconditions: ScriptSecurity implementation DefaultScriptSecurity is selected by the UserAgent.
The document URL or the script URL parses to a null host (e.g. data:, relative, or file-scheme references).
The script reference falls into the exempted branch (data protocol or equal URLs) or the identity/equals test otherwise evaluates false.
candidates.title: DefaultScriptSecurity host check can be bypassed when both hosts are null (identity comparison + null-host short-circuit)

counter_evidence: The class name and the separate EmbededExternalResourceSecurity strongly suggest that permitting data: URIs is intended behavior of the default implementation.
The identity/equals host comparison at lines 85-86 is consistent with the sibling class and may be adequate for the intended http(s) use cases.
No read code shows a caller passing an attacker-controlled null externalResourceURL, so the line-83 ordering concern may be unreachable.
candidates.description: DefaultExternalResourceSecurity is documented to allow external resources only from the same server as the document, but the check is bypassed for the data protocol: inside the differing-host branch, if externalResourceURL is non-null and its protocol equals DATA_PROTOCOL ("data"), no SecurityException is created (lines 88-94), regardless of how the host comparison resolved. Additionally, the host of externalResourceURL is dereferenced at line 83 (externalResourceURL.getHost()) before the null test for externalResourceURL at line 88, so the loop-guard ordering does not protect against a null externalResourceURL at line 83. The DATA_PROTOCOL exemption for external resources may be intentional (the EmbededExternalResourceSecurity class exists precisely to restrict to data:), but in DefaultExternalResourceSecurity the effect is that a data: URI is accepted even when the document host differs, which weakens the stated same-server policy and can interact with data-URI parsing/SSRF considerations. Reported as a candidate, not a confirmed vulnerability: the exemption may be by design, and callers were only seen via search excerpts.
missing_evidence: Which callers instantiate DefaultExternalResourceSecurity and under what URL shapes.
Whether the null-externalResourceURL ordering at lines 83/88 is reachable via a real input.
The full ParsedURL parsing semantics (authority/host handling) needed to know exactly when getHost() is null.
preconditions: DefaultExternalResourceSecurity is the selected ExternalResourceSecurity implementation.
The external resource reference resolves to a URL whose protocol is "data" while the document URL host differs (or is null).
The caller reaches checkLoadExternalResource() only after constructing the instance.
candidates.title: DefaultExternalResourceSecurity allows any `data:` external resource across hosts and dereferences URL before its null check

counter_evidence: The search excerpt indicates a static block disabling external-general-entities and external-parameter-entities, suggesting the hardening is present in this tree.
The read handler code (appendStringData, characters, processingInstruction, startDTD) performs no external dereference itself; it only builds DOM nodes.
No evidence in the read spans that the parserClassName branch is reachable from untrusted input.
candidates.description: The read spans of SAXDocumentFactory (1-200 and 560-759) show the SAX handler implementation, including startDTD (line 755-759), which stores the DTD name/publicId/systemId into a DocumentType that is then attached to the created document (doctype is used at line 639 via implementation.createDocument(nsURI, rawName, doctype)). The read spans do NOT contain the static configuration block that the search excerpt shows setting external-general-entities and external-parameter-entities to false; therefore the sufficiency of hardening (e.g., whether external DTD/schema access, DOCTYPE declarations, or feature-negotiation fallbacks such as accessExternalDTD are addressed) cannot be confirmed from source actually read. If any path reaches createDocument with a parser whose entity/DTD features are not disabled (e.g. the parserClassName branch invoked through XMLReaderFactory.createXMLReader(parserClassName), visible only in a search excerpt), external entity resolution could occur. This is flagged as a source-uncertainty / potential vulnerability rather than a demonstrated defect; the entity-disabling code was not inside an allowed read range.
missing_evidence: The exact parser configuration block (the search excerpt is not an allowed read span).
The createDocument(InputSource) method body that selects parserClassName vs saxFactory.newSAXParser().
Whether additional protections (disallow-doctype-decl, accessExternalDTD/accessExternalSchema, external entity resolver restrictions) are configured.
preconditions: A code path instantiates SAXDocumentFactory and parses untrusted XML/SVG.
The effective parser is created via a branch that does not inherit the disabled external-entity features.
The parsed document contains a DOCTYPE/entity that triggers external resolution.
candidates.title: Parser hardening in SAXDocumentFactory not verifiable from the read spans; DOCTYPE/systemId is still accepted into the DOM
